Madam Speaker, I rise in the House today to affirm that under this government the gap between the rich and the poor is widening at tremendous speed.
While the government plays with the unemployment insurance benefits, employment is suffering its largest drop since 1982 and the economy continues to show no signs of recovery. The Minister of Finance predicted at budget time that the unemployment rate would be 10 per cent, but as I speak today, it is much higher than 10 per cent.
I am afraid for the people of Prince Edward Island and for Canada. The Canadian Jobs Strategy fund has been cut by $100 million. Between April 1990 and January 1991, Canadians have lost 288,000 jobs. At a time when the people of Prince Edward Island need work to support their families, funds for new social housing have been reduced and Islanders have been forced out into the street.
Since 1984, the people of Prince Edward Island have come to expect economic hardships. How much more will this government ask Islanders to take before it stops catering to the rich and faces the real problems of the average Canadian.

Madam Speaker, when we are honouring Canadians for their efforts in the Persian Gulf war, let us not forget one of
Canada's great traditions, the Red Cross Society, leaders in international war relief.
To assist them in the role of the Persian Gulf, the federal government has pledged $4 million. In addition to this money, the society has launched a $1 million Persian Gulf appeal. So far individual Canadians, participating banks, provinces and territorial governments have contributed more than $370,000.
This year, 1991, marks the 95th anniversary of the Canadian Red Cross Society. This volunteer based organization, with over 3,000 volunteers in my city alone, provides emergency relief blood centres to 600 branches in more than 1,000 operating units.
It is particularly fitting at this time, when the original role of the Red Cross is highlighted by the gulf crisis, to invite all Canadians to congratulate the board members and the staff of volunteers of the Red Cross Society. They do a great service for Canada.

Madam Speaker, today's much-touted Clean Air Accord remains deficient; celebration is premature. The ceremonial signing offers appearance without substance, hiding government failings in a flashy replay of previous agreements.
Compliance mechanisms required from monitoring and enforcement remain window dressing at best. Transboundary pollution of Canadian lands by toxic chemicals continue to be a threat. Funding for energy conservation and alternatives to fossil fuels has been slashed. December's promise by the environment minister for national acid rain caps in the Green Plan has been forgotten. Federal air standard agreements with the three western provinces have not been achieved.
This accord may be better than nothing, however, it fails to prevent pollution or protect the health and environment of Canadians. It leaves Canada satisfied to follow the lead of the U.S. in setting standards for air emissions and fails to commit the resources to determine our own stringent regulations for the well-being of Canada's future.

Madam Speaker, to you, first of all, and your colleagues, my congratulations for the role you have played over the last decade in the long and difficult saga of reducing acid rain pollution in Canada.
As the Prime Minister and President Bush pose for a photo opportunity today, 3.2 million tonnes of sulphur dioxide pollution continue to cross from the U.S. to Canada every year. Put another way, in the 17 hours that President Bush is in Canada, over 6,000 tonnes of U.S. pollution will have crossed the border too. By 1995, 2.7 million tonnes per year will continue to drift our way and, by the year 2000, still two million tons.
Therefore, the Canadian public should keep in mind that the political accord signed today is only the first, not the final, step in the battle against transboundary acid rain. The next phase is to establish how much we must reduce acid gas emissions beyond the 50 per cent goal that was established a decade ago.
The acid rain battle is far from over.

The loan rate guides the price established on the Chicago grain market, and a modest increase of at least $1 a bushel in the loan rate would substantially raise world grain prices and reduce government deficiency payment expenditures to farmers.

Now, four years later, the United States is refusing to accept the January decision of the free trade dispute settling mechanism on Canadian pork exports.
Can the Minister for International Trade inform this House of the nature of the discussions between the Prime Minister and President Bush today on this most important matter?

speakerposition: Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the series of actions that we have taken together with Canadian pork producers in connection with pork has been an unparalleled example of success. We have been successful in the GATT panel with reference to this question. We have been successful
with respect to a panel under the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement.
Now, in desperation, the U.S. National Pork Producers Council has filed a petition asking United States trade representatives to establish an extraordinary challenge committee to review the panel's action. That is an act of desperation on its part. It is an extraordinary procedure the council is asking to be used which has not been used so far. It can only properly be used with respect to some misbehaviour of panel members. It is extremely unlikely, if the USTR gives permission for it to go forward, that it would be successful.
To date our record is unparalleled in the success we have had under the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement in this important area.

Madam Speaker, Canadian pork exported to the United States makes up about 3 per cent to 4 per cent of its total market, yet this harassment continues.

ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - VIOLENCE AGAINST WOMEN Ms. Mary Clancy (Halifax) moved:
That this House call upon the Prime Minister to appoint a royal
commission on violence against women.
She said: I rise today in support of this motion because the women of Canada are in crisis. It is unfortunate that it took the unmitigated tragedy of December 1989 in Montreal to bring to our attention the crisis facing Canadian women in the area of violence. In my party we call most strongly for the appointment of a royal commission on violence against women.
We are not alone in this call. We are supported by our colleagues to the left in the New Democratic Party. We are also supported by any number of women's groups, nationally, regionally and provintially, some of whom I will be speaking about later in my remarks.
I am going to go at this in a rather unusual way to begin, in that I am going to talk about the reasons against a royal commission.
One of the reasons most frequently cited since various women's groups and political parties have been calling for the establishment of such a commission has been the cost. There is no question when Canada is in a recession, when cutbacks are facing us all, that we all have to be concerned with the question of costs.
The second area with relation to costs has been raised again by a number of people. The cost of a royal commission would be better spent on direct services to women in crisis, to transition houses and so on.
Indeed, if I thought that kind of money would go in direct services, the kind of money it takes to run a royal commission, I might be briefly tempted to adhere to those beliefs myself. But it would be a brief temptation. I will go into the reason I say when I speak of the reasons for a royal commission.
But let me come up against some other criticisms. Frequently we hear that the reports of royal commissions are left to die on the shelves of libraries across the country. They gather dust or they are only partially implemented. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, that is true.
Just some royal commissions that have been left to this fate are the Cooke commission on child care in Canada, the Abella commission on employment equity, the Fraser commission on pornography and prostitution, and many, many sections of Senator Florence Bird's incredible and, if I may call it this, "the grandmother of royal
March 13, 1991

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
commissions", the 1970 Royal Commission on the Status of Women.
Royal commissions tend right now to be a bit in disfavour because of the Spicer Commission, which is irritating many Canadians because of what they see as amorphous and fuzzy national exercises in navel gazing. But a royal commission, constituted correctly, rooted in women's experience, with built-in guarantees can create the kind of action and the kind of success that we desperately need.
First of all, a royal commission on violence against women, before it is appointed, the Prime Minister and the government should engage in a wide consultation with front-line workers, with transition house staff, with sexual assault crisis centre workers, with women's centre workers, with police in those few municipalities with programs that truly identify problems and respond appropriately; and with academics in women's studies, sociology, anthropology, criminology and various other relevant departments.
I said that a number of women's groups, nation-wide, have been calling for the appointment of a royal commission on violence against women. Some of these groups are the YWCA of Canada, various advisory councils around the country, the Canadian Research Institution for the Advancement of Women and the Canadian Congress for Learning Opportunities for Women-just to name a few. They are calling for a royal commission, always provided that it is not a way to back-burner an issue that is facing us on a daily basis and threatening the lives of women.
The mandate of a royal commission must be to hear the experience of the victims, to determine empirically the incidence of violence against women. We suspect that as yet we cannot prove empirically that violence against women crosses all boundaries-economic, social, cultural and educational.
The royal commission must seek out the causes of violence against women. Is it related to alcohol and drug abuse? Is it stress related due to economic conditions? Is it rooted in the economic dependency of women? Is it rooted in the fact that women are, in general, physically weaker than men? Is there, indeed, one lowest common
Supply
denominator, or are there a variety of indicators and triggers?
Yesterday at the Subcommittee on Violence Against Women, Dr. Eileen Sanders of Carleton University's School of Journalism spoke to us on violence in the media.
One of the things she told us was that the traditional areas of research are inadequate to deal with this problem. In other words, the all-pervasiveness of violence, and in particular violence against women, in our society does not necessarily respond to old-style cause and effect research projects. We must look at a broader base and a broader experience of women throughout the country and of those who work with women in crisis to give us at least the beginning of the answers we need to construct the solutions.
Can we predetermine indicators of violence and can we thus educate and violence-proof our children to break what has become a vicious cycle of abuse in our society?
Ever since the Montreal massacre, women across the country, and men too, have been galvanized-academics, professionals, housewives-asking why. Why is it that our country and western society in general, indeed world society, is faced with what is a plague of violent behaviour of men toward women? Women are asking, perhaps in the saddest voices of all, how do we protect ourselves and how does society help us protect ourselves, most terribly from those we love?
Random violence in the street is terrifying, but how much more terrifying is violence against women which, like its antithesis, charity, appears to begin and flourish at home. It is a fact that in this country women are beaten and murdered primarily by their partners. One suspects, and I say again, this is the problem, suspicion is not empirical proof that the increasing violence against women by strangers, Marc Lepine, date rape, street attacks, stem from societal attitudes.
Clearly, to some extent, if women and beaten and harassed at home, and as a society we do nothing constructive to combat this, then an insidious belief that the battering of women is inconsequential becomes de facto a part of our communal fabric. We need desperate-

ly to shine the harsh light of reality on this dark side of our society, on this dark side of too many people's daily lives.
Again, we believe that a royal commission, travelling nation-wide, hearing evidence nation-wide, can do this where lesser initiatives cannot.
Many women committed to ending this horror say that money spent on a royal commission, as I said before, would be better spent on direct services. Let me state now that I, and my colleagues in this party, men and women, have and will continue to plead for money for services. It is a national scandal that 50 per cent of the women and their children who seek help from transition houses must be turned away. Yes, 50 per cent. That is both disgraceful and terrifying.
Remember, this is not an either/or situation. We desperately need both. We need transition houses, but we also need the research, the education and the publicity that a royal commission can engender.
We know, for example, that the province of Ontario in the last several years put on an excellent ad campaign to raise awareness of the battery of women. Hosts of women in that province, encouraged by these ads, came forward to seek assistance. They were turned away because the money, the beds, the facilities just were not there.
We also know that as yet many judges and legislators and police still do not react correctly. Every lawyer and social worker in this House knows the answer to this one. Police in general do not respond to domestic disputes as they do to other complaints. I recall one incident when a battered wife who had a court order from the Chief Justice. She called me on the phone and said her husband was banging down her kitchen door with a baseball bat, that she had the police department on the other line and they were saying to her: "How do we know you have a court order". I called them, identified myself, told them of the court order, gave them the date and all the relevant information and they still refused to come.
Fortunately, that particular incident did not end in actual physical abuse. But, I ask all members of this House to imagine the psychological abuse that took place from that encounter. Imagine the kind of faith that woman would have in our system after that took place.
Too many judges sentence when a conviction is obtained inappropriately. We cannot forget, and it is again to our national shame, that in this country in the last two years we heard one judge call a pre-school female child sexually provocative. We heard another judge state that sexual assaults on native women were less serious because the women may have been drinking or sleeping in a public place. Another judge in the province of Ontario implied that an exotic dancer, the victim of a sexual assault, had by reason of her employment invited the assault and thus gave up her right to say no.
As a nation, we must act now to stem this tide of violence. Those bright, ambitious and non-traditional young women who died so tragically at Ecole Polytechnique must be memorialized, but not by white roses, white ribbons or plaques, but by remedies.
We cannot restore their lives. We cannot return them to their families, to their beginning careers, to their friends, nor can we restore the lives of the other 119 women who died in 1989 in Canada at the hands of their partners.
The other day, in questioning the Prime Minister about the economic situation facing women in this country, he responded with a list of appointments made by the federal government of women to boards, commissions, to the courts and so on. I have applauded every one of those appointments, but that was not the issue. The issue is ostensibly economic and, I believe, inextricably wrapped up with the issue of violence is the position of women in our society.
I would like to respond to the Prime Minister with a few facts of my own from the Index on Canadian Women, published in December 1990.
We already know, we have heard it ad nauseam, that Statistics Canada reports that women still earn only 66 cents for every dollar earned by men, that Canadian women face a higher risk of being poor than men. The National Council of Welfare reports that in 1987, 57 per cent of single mothers lived below the poverty line and that 1,515,000 Canadian women lived in poverty. That was four years ago. We were not in a recession in 1987. How much worse are those figures today?
Statistics Canada figures for 1988 show a high proportion of women, 17.2 per cent, have less than a grade nine education, and that 84 per cent of Canadian women working outside the home are employed in service

speechtext:
industries and concentrated in non-unionized, lower paying occupations.
In 1988, 28.2 per cent of female workers were clerical workers. In 1986, 1,001,340 clerical workers worked part-time or part-year and earned salaries that were below the national poverty level. Only 36 per cent of women covered by the Employment Equity Act earn over $27,500, compared to 80 per cent of men; 28 per cent of aboriginal women, compared to 72 per cent of aboriginal men; 38 per cent of disabled women, compared to 81 per cent of disabled men earn over this figure and 28 per cent of visible minority women, as compared to 73 per cent of visible minority men earn over this figure.
In 1989, three out of four Canadian women in prime child-bearing and raising age groups, 20 to 45, were in the labour force. Adequate child care has become less accessible rather than more accessible.
By 1989, there were 450,000 more pre-school children with mothers in the labour force without licensed child care than there were in 1979. In 1987, only 8 per cent of children with working mothers were cared for in licensed child care services.
One in four Canadian women are sexually abused at some time in their lives, half before they reach the age of 17. One in ten women are beaten by their male partners. In the last two years in Canada, over 100 women per year have been killed by their male partners.
Twenty years after the Royal Commission on the Status of Women, women are still not even close to being equal participants. Of the 167 recommendations made in that royal commission, only 55 have been implemented.
Last week I was accused of being negative. I guess I have to plead guilty to that. The truth is that the vast majority of Canadian women do not share in the Canadian dream. They live in poverty and work in job ghettos. They cannot move freely in our society. Every woman in this House as well as every woman watching this and every woman in this country, whether she admits it or not, is vulnerable to violence.
Supply
Project Haven and the recent initiatives announced by the Minister of National Health and Welfare are well intentioned. I have no doubt of that, but they are criminally inadequate.
The workers on the front lines are themselves overworked, underpaid and subject to burnout from the enormity of the task they are attempting to perform.
Last week in response to a question, I was as I said, accused of being negative. Again, I say I plead guilty. The violence experienced by women in Canada is inextricably tied to economics, to discrimination on the basis of sex and to the failure of all governments to take meaningful action.
Yes, the country is burdened with a deficit. Yes, we must be sound fiscal managers. Yes, we must keep our house in order financially, but a government that preaches these truisms must also remove its blinkers. If women, who make up 52 per cent of our population, cannot enjoy basic security of the person, and if their government ignores their crisis, it does not seem to me to be much of a government.
We need immediate and concrete action. Groups across this country ciy out for a royal commission on violence against women. We need to find answers, solutions and a resolution of the problem. If we ignore these cries, we do not deserve the title of representatives of the people.

Mr. Speaker, I obviously know of the hon. member's interest in this subject.
I wonder if she has given any thought to ways in which provincial and territorial governments might be involved in a royal commission, being aware, as she indicated, that this is not an issue that the federal government alone can solve or deal with.
If as a result of some of the presentations she has heard at the standing committee she could give any advice in this area, it would be appreciated.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. minister for her question.
One of the things that I think is very interesting is taking place in my province of Nova Scotia. It has been recommended and I hope it is taking place. We have not heard definitely yet on a response.

March 13, 1991

Debbie Forsythe Smith, president of the Nova Scotia Advisory Council on the Status of Women, has asked for a review. At the time that she asked for the review, there had been five murders with the same profile-women murdered by their partners-in under two years.
Tragically, there have been two more murders in the last month in the metropolitan area of Halifax-Dartmouth. Indeed, there was another one shortly after I spoke last week.
Deborah Forsythe Smith and her council have asked the Attorney General of Nova Scotia to set up a special review commission to look at these five murders in particular to try to find if there is a common denominator and if there are indicators that could give us some idea of how to anticipate and possibly prevent this kind of behaviour.
There was some comment by the Attorney General in Nova Scotia, but there has not yet been a final response. I would hope they would do that. I would see that as something that could feed very well into a royal commission in the sense that a royal commission, of course, does not just hold hearings, it also commissions reports and takes reports from whatever source. I would think that a report such as this in Nova Scotia would be invaluable.
I would also think that a response to the situation in Ontario, following that ad campaign, would be of great assistance as well, because a number of witnesses who have come to us at the committee talked about how particularly well done the Ontario ad campaign was. I had a very special feeling about that. A good friend of mine, an actress whom I had worked with, was one of the main actors in those ads. It was very moving, very compelling and communicated the thought well. As I say, the response from the people was overwhelming, but the facilities were not there. I would think the Ontario government could be of help.
A third response to that relates to the whole question of native women. When we had native women appearing before the committee several weeks ago, they talked about the special needs of native and northern women in this area. I think this is something to which we must be extremely sensitive and, indeed, it may well be that we discover what works for women in urban centres like Halifax, Toronto, Montreal and so on, will not work in
rural Canada, will not work with native aboriginal women and will not work perhaps with immigrant women. That is why this royal commission must be rooted in women's experience to bring across, as Dr. Saunders, from Carleton, said yesterday, "a new form of research that really hits the problem".

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Halifax gave a vibrant and compelling testimony in support of the motion put forward by the official opposition, the Liberal Party of Canada, which reads:
That this House call upon the Prime Minister to appoint a Royal
Commission on Violence Against Women.
I have here, on my desk, a huge file on the subject, Mr. Speaker. I have always taken an interest in this matter. In my riding, we have the Maison de I'Amitie, or friendship house, a shelter for battered women, and I have to admit that, even then, one shelter does not seem to be enough. I think we would need two of them.
I was impressed by the comment made by my colleague from Halifax who stated that 50 per cent of the women and their children who seek help cannot have or are denied access to shelters. I share her concern for the serious problems facing the million or so Canadian women and children who are abused every year by a spouse. I also agree with her that, in our career as members of Parliament, we have all seen various cases of cruel and even sadistic treatment, Mr. Speaker, inflicted upon too many women and children.
I have a question to ask the hon. member because she mentioned in her speech that perhaps we should consider broadening the mandate of this royal commission to include the effects of violence in order to prevent it and involving as many Canadians, men and women, in this much needed process.

I received, just in the last day or so, a letter from the Federation of Women Teachers' Associations of Ontario. I think she is familiar with that organization. It concerns their desire to establish a royal commission on violence against women, to which they attach a long list of groups and organizations which support this proposal.
March 13, 1991

I just want to ask the member one question. In asking for a comprehensive study on the subject of violence, does she agree that we should at least involve as many Canadians as possible and that we want to prevent violence, not just deal with its consequences? Does she agree with this group of people, the Federation of Women Teachers' Associations, that it is imperative for us to address this system?

I thank my colleague, the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier, for his comments.
Indeed I agree most strongly with the Ontario women teachers association. I am happy to say that its representatives have spoken to us and have been witnesses before the subcommittee on the status of women on the topic of violence against women.
They have as well in the province of Ontario, through the good offices of Ontario teachers, come up with a number of programs in the schools. This relates as well to the minister's question. This kind of program can be of tremendous value, shared across the country.
The creation of a royal commission can solve a problem that many of the front-line workers against violence against women have told us about, that is that there is no mechanism for them to communicate with each other at the moment. If persons working in a transition house in Nova Scotia could communicate with their colleagues in British Columbia, Ontario, Quebec, and so on, it would be of invaluable assistance and the data collected would be tremendous. The exchange of programs such as the kind the Ontario teachers have come up with would be of great assistance to the Nova Scotia Teachers Union, B.C. teachers, and so on and so forth.
It is the need to pull all this material together, to pull together the kind of research that is necessary to get at this all-pervasive problem, that causes women such as those in the Ontario Women Teachers Federation and the other groups I have mentioned, such as the YWCAs and so on, to call for this commission.

Mr. Speaker, I congratulate my colleague from Halifax for bringing this motion forward to the House of Commons. It is essential that we debate this issue.

We sit together on a subcommittee of health and welfare, the subcommittee on the status of women that is right now hearing witnesses on violence against women. We have been hearing various groups from across the country-transition home workers, teachers, some victims of violence themselves, and religious people working to provide assistance to women who are battered. We have heard from a cross-section of Canadian women on this issue.
What does the hon. friend feel is the underlying theme that we are hearing over and over again from these presentations? How would she respond to my concern about the systemic discrimination against women in our society and how that contributes toward the whole issue of violence against women?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for New Westminster-Burnaby for her question.
That in a sense is the whole root and branch of the issue. We live in a society that is systemically discriminatory against women. Indeed, I look around this House right now and I count six women sitting in seats, duly elected, and I think: wow, are we ever lucky that we are here, because the odds were sure against us; all of us, no matter what party we belong to, and I think we all know it.
That is why I rhymed off all those horrific statistics that I mentioned before. The problem is that systemic discrimination against women is intrinsically economic. It is rooted in patriarchy and it is rooted, with the greatest of respect and affection to the vast majority of my male colleagues, in a lack of understanding on the part of the people who truly wield the power.
In the vast majority of cases, I think men do not really comprehend how deeply rooted discrimination against women is. It is so deeply rooted, it is so much a part of our society and the way we live, it is so utterly a part of their daily lives, that they cannot see the forest for the trees. Until those of us who are lucky enough to crash through these barriers and make our voices heard, make those voices loud enough and united enough to bring these issues home, we are still going to be voices ciying in the wilderness.
