speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the chance to join in the debate on this issue this afternoon. It is very important that we debate an issue as fundamental to society as violence against women. It is an issue which I would hope members on all sides of the House are concerned about, care about, and are prepared to join in finding solutions.
While it is an issue that women have primarily brought to the public agenda and have brought to the public fore, it is absolutely essential that men understand and become involved in this issue. We need their co-operation and understanding, as my hon. colleague has just talked about, if we are to make some of the fundamental changes and attitudinal changes, in society which are going to enable us to one day eliminate violence against women.
Violence against women is not only physical violence when we talk about the issue at large. Physical violence is often the final result of many years or months of emotional abuse which many women suffer, whether it is in a marriage, another family situation, or with a partner with whom they are living. We have to understand that when we are talking about violence against women, we also have to include that kind of emotional, psychological abuse which many workers in this field that I have talked with say can often have more devastating long-term impacts on women because it so destroys their sense of self-esteem and self-worth that they do not find any way of getting out of those situations.
Physical abuse, yes. That is absolutely heinous in every way, but we have to find ways to address emotional abuse as well.
It is important to understand the statistics, to know just how grave this situation is across Canada. From the various studies and reports that we have been able to put together from Status of Women-and there has been a number of works done both in Canada and elsewhere- the most commonly known statistics at this time indicate that one in four women will be sexually assaulted at some time in her life, and that half of the sexual assaults will be perpetrated on women under the age of 17. That includes the issue of sexual abuse of female children, which is so appalling, and of teenage women as well.
Statistics show that one in ten women in Canada is assaulted by her husband or partner, and that half the women in Canada are afraid to go out after dark in their own neighbourhoods. Rightly or wrongly, that is the perception they have. I would imagine that all women in this House have felt that at certain times. I know I have in certain situations, certain cities that I have lived in. If I can't be as free as a man to go out and be able to participate in every aspect of society, that denies me my freedom and my equality.
We also know that one homicide in five in this country is a family violence homicide. Also, about 4 per cent of seniors now report being abused, which is a whole new issue. As violence against women was not talked about 20 years ago in the royal commission on the status of women, it is only in the last five years that the whole issue of abuse of seniors has really been talked about. That includes physical violence and also emotional abuse of seniors as well.
One study of disabled women found that almost half of disabled women had been sexually abused as children, that one in four were sexually assaulted as an adult, and that most of these women had been abused by their caretakers. We could rhyme off these statistics, but when we think of the devastation of the lives of these women behind these statistics, it gets pretty emotional as far as I am concerned. I am sure we have all known women who have been victims of violence. We have probably known the perpetrators as well in different instances.
My colleague mentioned aboriginal women. The statistics there are even more horrendous, some as high as eight out of ten aboriginal women have been sexually assaulted or have been physically abused at some time in their lives. And we know what that leads to.
It is not only the physical, the emotional harm that is done to women through violence. It leads to inequality. It is almost a chicken and egg situation: inequality that leads to the violence but violence then leads to inequality. It leads to the diminution of self-esteem, self-worth, and the ability of women then to get themselves out of situations. Without the kind of support that many women's organizations, shelters, and crisis lines across the country have provided, many of these women would continue to live in silence and terror. I think it has been only 18 years since the first women's shelter was opened
March 13, 1991

in Canada. They have done an enormously important and successful job, and we all applaud those efforts.
Certainly the goal of federal and provincial governments everywhere has to be to work toward the achievement of equality of all citizens in our society. I guess I perceive Canadian society, despite the dark and gloomy statistics that I have just reported on violence, as being one of the most fortunate societies around the world. When I had the opportunity last fall to chair the Commonwealth Women's Affairs Ministers' meeting, in recognizing of most of the countries that we were dealing with around the Commonwealth we were indeed more fortunate in this country. We had the legal mechanisms. We had more economic and social equality than even some of our closest friends in countries like Australia. Yet we know there are ways to go. Elow do we work toward achieving that equality?
Certainly one way is by having women here in this House of Commons as role models and being able to speak out to show women across the country that it is possible for women to be involved in the decision-making processes of this country. We want to encourage that in every possible way, as I know all my colleagues do from whatever party they represent, that we need more women in this House of Commons, in legislatures and in municipal councils who understand and can raise these issues at every level.
Our Prime Minister quoted statistics the other day about the numbers of women in various government positions. I know in a sense that those are just numbers, but they are important because they are again showing women as role models. We see that women have now gone from 37 to 83 in judicial postings and that women now are holding judgeships at the federal level within our system and are having an influence. We have seen women assuming positions of responsibility in the Public Service at the deputy minister level. Women have increased from 7 to 24 as the heads of missions at the diplomatic level. All those kinds of examples are important because they too become role models.
When we look at the kind of initiatives that have been taken over these past few years to move toward economic equality, each one of those is a step and part of the road to progress of economic equality. Some might say
Supply
that it has not been fast enough but always there is balance.
We have moved forward on employment equity. We have moved forward on pay equity. We have moved forward on changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act in areas such as maternity benefits. We have moved forward indeed on family violence.
Three years ago was the first time that a federal government initiated a family violence program with $40 million. As a result of that program we are seeing a lot of the action. We are seeing a lot of activity generated across the country, which is raising the voices of women and making people aware of this issue.
I was looking at a report on the funding that has been provided in the last four years. The types of projects are fascinating: everything from workshops in Stony Rapids, Saskatchewan on the prevention of family violence to the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police. Obviously that is an area where police have to become more effective in their intervention work. The Provincial Advisory Council of Newfoundland has established an inter-agency commission to create a model of co-ordinated activity against family violence. There are projects in my home province of British Columbia dealing with disabled women. There have been 600 or 700 projects funded-some for a couple of thousand dollars, some for hundreds of thousands of dollars-as we work forward toward investigating areas of research, prevention, education and support services.
Obviously more needs to be done because still violence persists. We have only just started to skim the surface in our understanding. I do not think we have a full understanding of what it is that creates or triggers a male to become the batterer or assaulter. We know that statistics show about 85 per cent of violence against women is related to those in trust and about 15 per cent to those who are unknown to the women.
What is it? Is it frustration? Is it indeed the fact that women are perceived as both physically less equal and in some ways economically or psychologically less equal? There are all those kinds of issues. We know that there is a generational component to this as well. Both the abusers and those who are victims of abuse are more likely to continue that into the next generation. We have to find ways of breaking that cycle of violence within our society.

March 13, 1991
Supply
We know there is a need to review our laws. My colleague, the Minister of Justice, today in Vancouver made some announcements about some of the initiatives she will be taking in the criminal justice system to review our laws and to work with judges, the Solicitor General and law enforcement agencies to be more effective in dealing with family violence. This is all part of the new $136 million program that my colleague, the Minister of National Health and Welfare announced two weeks ago. I know he will be talking about that a little later.
We know there has been a lot done in education. The program in Ontario was mentioned. I agree that was an excellent program. The province of Quebec has undertaken education programs, the province of British Columbia has as well. Yukon territory has just announced a fascinating new policy dealing with family violence. It is probably the most comprehensive policy statement I have seen in this country and deals with all facets of it. Those kinds of initiatives at provincial and territorial levels are very important.
We need education of our young people. The Canadian Teachers Federation project "Thumbs Down" will take into the schools programs to help children right from kindergarten all the way up to understand the root causes of violence, to deal themselves with how they might react in violent situations, to be able to say no, and to understand that violence is not acceptable in our society. That is an important part of the whole puzzle we are dealing with as well.
My federal and provincial colleagues, including myself as Minister responsible for the Status of Women, last May produced what we called The Lake Louise Declaration on Family Violence, in which we have agreed to work together to develop a national strategy. Our officials have been working on that. We are planning to bring it forward later this spring when we meet again in Newfoundland and to find ways to co-ordinate our efforts so that at the federal, provincial and territorial levels we will tiy not to duplicate or overlap our efforts and to see what are the gaps.
We have just recently commissioned through Status of Women Linda MacLeod, one of the foremost experts in this country on family violence, to do a review for us, a kind of a pre-study to indicate what in her opinion are the gaps in terms of research and what are the mechanisms we should be looking at to move forward.
I do not think there is any doubt in my mind or in the minds of anyone in this House that we need mechanisms to move forward in our understanding of this issue. I would ask my colleagues who sit on the subcommittee on the status of women and are examining this issue to give us their advice on the kinds of mechanisms that are most appropriate. If we are talking about a royal commission, I worked for a royal commission for four years so I have a somewhat jaundiced view in that I do not think four years is necessary to get on with some of the actions required.
We need innovative approaches, whether it is through a royal commission or other kinds of mechanisms, to reach out to women; not just sitting around hotel rooms and having regular hearings but mechanism by which we can actually find out from women what their experiences are and be able to make women feel comfortable in relaying those kinds of experiences to some kind of initiative that might help us understand the issue as well.
Obviously what I would like to see is something that is cost effective, that does not duplicate what is already being done, and that can help us move forward, maybe on a step-by-step basis. I would like to see something for which we do not have to wait until the end to finally have action. I would like to see us not have to set up whole new infrastructures to deal with an issue where there are perhaps some existing infrastructures through the National Advisory Council or groups like that, where we might be able to do things more effectively and perhaps from a feminist point of view and not just copy-cat what has been done in the past, but think creatively of how we can address this issue most effectively in the future.
We need a focus on research. I have met with the Canadian Association of University Teachers on some of their proposals for centres of excellence. They are working now with the Social Science and Humanities
March 13, 1991

Research Council on those. We have existing groups out there that I think we could bring together.
As I indicated, because many of the things that need to be done in terms of service delivery, fall primarily within the jurisdiction of the provinces, we obviously need their involvement, co-operation and support. There is no sense spending time and putting forward recommendations when there is no one there to pick them up and run with them. As I mentioned, the province of British Columbia has just recently set up a task force on family violence. The province of Manitoba is doing some work in that area as well, and as colleague mentioned, the province of Nova Scotia is also active in that area.
Maybe we can find a way of linking all these activities together so they are not all going off separately and ensuring that again we are not overlapping, not duplicating, but we are trying to get to the real core of the subject.
When thinking about some of the things that need to be done-and I do not pretend to be an expert; I do not imagine any of us are experts in this field- and from my own experiences of talking to women who are both victims of violence and those who work with women at the grass roots level, many of them have said to me that we really have to do more with our young people, that is the age we really have to start addressing on this issue.
I feel more needs to be done with the media. So many of the messages our children get about the values of our society and on issues of equality of men and women, or on issues of violence, come from the media. Surely there are some ways we can bring the media together, to be involved in helping us to deal with these issues.
I am sure my hon. colleagues know these same stories, and it is not only from a personal point of view and my daughter's point of view, but others that I meet, there is something that seems to happen often to young girls between the ages of 12 and 14 that somehow their sights become diminished and from that stage on there is a transition where, often their own sense of equality changes. How do we get to young women at that age, to stop that from happening? The editorial in this month's Chatelaine deals with that issue and I think is a very interesting comment as well.
Supply
So we have to deal with our young people if we are going to look at education and prevention. We also have to look at whether there are really effective measures that we can take to deal with abusers or potential abusers. The jury is still out. I have heard reports both ways, as to whether some of the rehabilitation programs are effective or not. Some seem to be, some do not seem to be. Again, if we are going to deal with this issue with our present population, we have to find out what it is that works, that can trigger a change in behaviour among abusers or potential abusers.
So the challenge is there. It is a challenge for us all to work on. I am delighted with the work that my colleagues are doing, the Minister of National Health and Welfare, through Indian Affairs, $36 million that will be made available for aboriginal communities to decide for themselves how they want to deal with the issue of violence within their communities, both child sexual abuse and family violence. I know they have welcomed that, and we can use these resources over the next four years to take some significant steps forward.
I also welcome other ideas and suggestions of mechanisms by which we can develop our understanding and do it effectively without stalling on the progress that needs to be made.
Neither I nor any of the women here want to be sitting here four years from now, as I am sure we all shall be, and feel that we have not made any substantial progress.
So I would ask all colleagues to join together so that we can say, as a Canadian society, no to violence against women, that it is not acceptable in our society and that we can work together to change the attitudes, the causes and put in place those measures that can truly ensure that Canada is a place where women can be truly free and truly equal and free from violence.

Mr. Speaker, family violence is a social problem. It is the outward sign of some attitudes, such as sexism, ageism, and tolerance toward violence.
No social group, no socio-economic group, no culture and no region is safe from family violence. It is a challenge to our traditional approach with regard to prevention, protection, and treatment.

March 13, 1991
Supply
Assistance programs for the victims involve several service networks and institutions. Twenty years after the last public inquiry on this issue, we must all work together, Madam Speaker, because of the complex needs and different cultural backgrounds of the victims.

Those words are from the government's own document on family violence. If the minister really believes that, knowing our cultural communities, our adverse and diverse cultures today, a lot of violence is propagated there, how can you say that we are prepared to just go at it without having someone study the situation? Then we may be able to shame those that need the help and the communities that have to give the help into doing something about it.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I will respond to the hon. member and say, yes, indeed. I think it is very important for the public to understand that violence against women knows no economic bounds. Sometimes people think, well that only happens to poor women. That is not true. I know in my own region that the women who go to clinics are often professional women living with professional husbands.
It does not necessarily relate to one's socioeconomic background. Certainly in terms of the different ethnic communities in our country, one of the things we do know is that many of the women in those communities have been more afraid of coming out. Many of them have come from a culture where violence perhaps has been tolerated, are not aware that in our society it is not tolerated and are not aware of the services that are available. It has been good to see, for example, the province of Ontario's program. All of their materials are being made available in a number of languages so that they, hopefully, can get into those places in the community where women can access them.
A lot of research has been done. I would want to say to the hon. member that if she looks through the listing of studies and research that have been done in universities and by other organizations, a lot of work has been done and a lot is known. I am not sure it has all been put together and integrated in some way that enables us to be most effective. That is why, as I mentioned earlier, we have asked Linda McLeod, who is one of the experts in this field, to help us with this process over the next
month or so, and we might have a better understanding at Status of Women of where we should go next. We do not want to spend money uselessly on research that has already been undertaken.
There obviously are areas where research is required and probably areas where it would not be that helpful. We have to be able to use our resources effectively to find the answers that are still unknown.

It is
really interesting to sit today and listen to the member for Halifax and the minister who is from my province of British Columbia.
As I sat here, I could not help but wonder: If the positions were reversed, if women had the majority of seats in this House of Commons and if men were only 14 per cent of the members of the House, perhaps this issue would get the full attention that it needs. I just had to say that.
I listened to the minister carefully. She talked about the chicken and egg scenario and the evidence was not clear on whether violence leads to inequality or whether it is the inequality that leads to violence. I believe very clearly that is the inequality, the sexism and the misogyny that we see in our society that extends itself to violence against women. I would like her to kind of expand on the either/or statement that she made.
The other comment that I have is that the minister talked about the 14 per cent of us who are here in this place being role models for other Canadian women. I do not want to be a role model any more. My mother had role models. She had Agnes MacPhail and Grace Macln-nis. I had role models. I had Pauline Jewett and Margaret Mitchell. Darn it, it is time that we no longer look for role models, but we look for equality in society where women participate in every sector of our society on an equal and just basis.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I think the reality is that, as young people grow up, they do need role models. That is not necessarily sexist. It is in all aspects of life. They look to adults as role models. As we know, back in the 1940s and 1950s the only roles that women were playing were homemakers. That was the kind of role that they anticipated they would play.
March 13, 1991

Men need role models, too. It would be nice to have a lot more. I know that all my hon. colleagues would work towards that end. It is still going to be a while.
In terms of which leads to which, I think there is both.
I have known women who I would have perceived felt totally equal in all sorts of ways and yet, as a result of violence that was perpetrated, it was so demoralizing and created such a terrible trauma that they were not able to operate continuously in that manner.
It can have that effect individually on women as well, particularly as I mentioned, the kind of emotional abuse to which many women are subjected. A young women, through her teenage life and then enters into a marriage supposedly thinking it is all going to be wonderful, finds out that the partner is the kind of person who is constantly putting her down. Nothing is right. The house is not clean. The supper is not ready. These things may sound trivial, in a way. Finally, they just bear down on someone who is constantly being criticized.
I think one thing we tend to do in our society is criticize people too much. As young women, as teenagers they are constantly being criticized. If someone is always being criticized it is very difficult to develop one's ov,n sense of self-worth.
I might extrapolate that to this Chamber. If we did not criticize each other as much as my hon. colleague from Rosedale said last week, maybe we could move on in a much more positive way for the improvement of all members of society as a whole.

Mr. Speaker, want to make a couple of comments and put a question to the hon. member.
The disadvantage of following the hon. member for New Westminster-Burnaby is that she took the words right out of my mouth. I was going to say that until such time as there are more women in this House, equality will never be there.
I made a comment when I was speaking on the abortion issue earlier this year about how if men were able to conceive, we would never even discuss an abortion bill. I think it is the case that if men were on the receiving end of the majority of violence today, the laws punishing the offenders would be much stricter than they are. I think it is a shame that sometimes men who
Supply
commit violence against women are not given enough time in jail to reflect on their offences.
I just wanted to ask, and this may seem like an unfair question to the member, because I am not sure whether she was as member at the time, but some years ago in the House one of the members-the party really does not matter, but it was the party that this hon. minister belongs to-one of the members committed spousal assault and was convicted of that spousal assault. However, I do not think strong enough measures were taken to ensure that this member would understand the feelings against spousal assault. I wonder whether she would be willing to entertain, and I think most people would, that a member of the House should be evicted or ousted who commits spousal assault or violence against women?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I think there are mechanisms in the House by which the House manages its own affairs and so it would be inappropriate I think as a minister to be commenting on that.
I would like to comment on your earlier point though, because we do not have as many women in the House as we would like. We have to ensure that the men in the House understand and appreciate the issues that we were talking about. Perhaps there is a special burden on the men in the House to really take the time to make sure that they get out in their communities and visit the shelters, visit the women's centres, talk to women who are victims and show that as male members of Parliament they are as committed to dealing with this issue both in your personal behaviour and in your behaviour as a member of Parliament and are committed to coming back to the House to support us as women in our efforts to eradicate violence in Canadian society.

Mr. Speaker, in 1989, 119 women were murdered in domestic violence. Wife battering is a national disgrace. It is epidemic. Two and a half million Canadian women are beaten by their male partners and in many ways society closes its eyes.
Just over a year ago on December 6, 1989, one man gunned down 14 young women at the Ecole Polytechnique in Montreal and the country was in shock. Journalists, commentators, politicians all tried to make sense out of this horror. But few could accept the fact that he killed these young women simply because they were women, women he targeted as feminists. How many Canadians know that more women were killed by their male

March 13, 1991
Supply
partners in 1990 in Montreal than were murdered at the Ecole Polytechnique?
There is an urgent need to balance programs that treat today's violence with programs that prevent future tragedy. Women and children are in danger now. Transition houses, aggressive charging practices, counselling of victims and offenders all recognize the problem, yet they are not enough. They treat the result of violence, but they do not challenge the root of violence in our society, violence against women and children.
Prevention is an overwhelming challenge. We have heard it spoken about here today on both sides of the House. It is a massive challenge for our society. But violence against women is endemic in our culture.
Sexism and misogyny exist in newspapers, videos, rock videos, films, newspapers, ads, virtually eveiywhere. The images that our society sees on a daily basis are images that include violence against women.
Violence against women is the horrible extension of sexism in our society. It is sexism and misogyny taken to its worst degree, this most horrific degree and it is increasing.
Concentration on intervention alone marginalizes the victims. We have all heard the line: They deserved it; they should have left; they should never have married a man like that-and on and on it goes.
Yet we know that it is not a marginal problem. Conservative estimates tell us that one in 10 Canadian women in Canada today are beaten by their male partners. One in four women or girls are sexually assaulted. In 1988 15 per cent of all Canadian homicide victims were women killed by their male partners.
In 1988, according to the Canadian Centre for Justice statistics, 75,921 men were charged with assault, including wife abuse.
In 1987, the Ontario Ministry of the Attorney General reported 16,282 domestic assaults, and in 93.5 per cent of those assaults, those charged were male.
One of every two women and her children are turned away from transition houses in Canada because of a lack of space. Where do they go? Where do they end up? We know that the rate is even higher in some sections of this country. That is the national rate.
Women still earn on average 65 cents on every dollar that men earn, and we know that that wage gap has widened in the last two years. It was 66 cents, it has got worse. We are not making the kinds of economic gains for women that we know are so necessary and we know are part of the root of all of this problem of inequality and women's sense of powerlessness in our society.
Yet this government refuses to take strong and effective action on the issue of violence against women. Last month the government announced $136 million over four years for a family violence initiative. This means $15 million will be spent in the year 1991-92; $34 million in 1992-93; and the remainder allocated for after the term of this government ends.
But the real priorities of the government are revealed in their budget that was released a couple of weeks ago; a continuation of the cap on the Canada Assistance Plan, a decapitation of the Canada Assistance Plan, which is the federal-provincial funding mechanism that currently funds shelters for battered women, counselling for both victims and abusers, sexual assault centres, child care spaces, child welfare services. All were funded under the Canada Assistance Plan.
It seems that this government gives a drop in the bucket to the women of Canada one day and then empties the bucket a day or so later.
It is clear what is needed. We must increase shelter spaces and second-stage housing for battered women. We must provide funding to regional associations of battered women's houses so that these people can communicate and get the message out and understand what is going on in their communities and how it relates to the situation in other parts of Canada.
We need a comprehensive education program which includes mandatory gender sensitivity training for judges and for police forces and all of our judiciary.
We need flexible community-based programs for our rural areas.
March 13, 1991

We must recognize our multicultural diversity in this area. We must recognize it when we are providing programs and these programs must be developed in consultation with those communities. We must combat violence in the media. The minister spoke earlier of violence in the media. We know that the Ontario native women's association tells us that eight out of ten native women are battered. This is horrific. We must listen to native women and we must act. I acknowledge that the program introduced by the government does give an opportunity for the native people themselves to have input into that program.
I sit on the status of women subcommittee of the standing committee on health and welfare. I wish that the status of women committee were a standing committee, as it was in past Parliaments. It is not now; it is a subcommittee. We are now conducting hearings on violence against women. We have listened. We have listened to women from shelters for battered women; we have listened to women in the Canadian Teachers Association who have produced a great resource called "Thumbs Down", a classroom response toward violence against women. We have listened to the Federation of Women Teachers' Associations of Ontario which has also put out a document and a newsletter outlining all of the problems and concerns. Things are happening at the educational level of young people in our society. The professional associations are taking their responsibilities seriously on the issue of violence against women and working toward dealing with it in an educational sense in the classrooms.
We talk about the statistics in the House, and all of us who have spoken today on this issue have raised the statistics. While sitting in that committee room, I heard individual women from every region of the country tell us the same things. The women who work in the transition homes virtually said the same things. When the women from British Columbia spoke, they were surprised when we told them that the women from the Atlantic region had said the same thing or that the women from Ontario had said the same thing: that they were experiencing second generation abuse of families, and that they were both experiencing the same kinds of needs and seeing the same kinds of problems.
I think virtually all of the organizations that appeared before the subcommittee called for a royal commission on violence against women. I support their call for a royal commission. I support it wholeheartedly, and the
Supply
New Democratic Party supports it. We also called for a royal commission on violence against women some time ago.
It must be more than simply a public relations exercise. It cannot exist at a cost to essential services, some of the services that I have already talked about: shelters for battered women, counselling, educational services. And it most of all cannot be an excuse for lack of action.
It must be mandated to explore all aspects of violence against women, including the systemic causes of sexism in our society. It must deal with the issue of economics and the fact that women are not equal economic partners in our society, and that much of the violence against women results from this inequality. The commission must be made up of professionals and workers who deal with violence against women, who understand the issues surrounding violence against women, and it should also be made up of women who themselves have been victims of this violence. I think that the commission should be at least 50 per cent female.
I am pleased to support this call for a royal commission. I would urge the government to take this call seriously, which has grassroots support right across Canada. We do know that the Royal Commission on the Status of Women which was held some 20 years ago did serve a purpose. It pulled Canadian women together. I remember when that commission was being held, as a young woman in Vancouver, who was at home with three young children and whose own consciousness around these issues had not been raised at that point.
I remember hearing about this commission that was travelling across the country and the issues they were raising that were of concern to women. I think we can achieve the same kinds of educational benefits from a royal commission on violence against women.
The minister spoke of educating and encouraging males in our society, in our House of Commons, to take on this issue, to understand this issue and take some responsibility for finding a solution in our society for violence against women and children. I think that a royal commission would serve that purpose. I think it would be a wonderful educational tool. It would travel to every section of Canada and listen to women's voices, listen to the women who work in the field and educate the men in our society as well about the horrors of violence against

March 13, 1991
Supply
women and just how much, in real terms, it costs our society in every way.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the member. I know she has been a very active participant in the subcommittee dealing with this issue. As I mentioned, we will look forward to its report which I hope will give some definition to the specific areas it thinks require further study.
I just want to make one comment. The member, in her statement, indicated that the CAP payments through which much of the money flows for support of shelters had been cut. I just like to remind the hon. member that, indeed, is not correct. CAP payments have not been cut. They continue to grow. In the wealthy provinces of Ontario and Alberta and British Columbia, they continue to grow at 5 per cent, and in the other provinces continue their full growth. So, I would not see that should have any impact on the provinces' ability to continue their funding, as I would certainly encourage them to do.
The question I have for my colleague has to do with something I read in the paper this morning and I was really quite shocked. I am sure that my colleague is as well. In the NDP government in the province of Ontario, the consumer affairs minister, as I understand it, who last week posed as a "Sunshine Boy", is now purported to have an assistant who, indeed, had been charged and convicted of wife battering and is now working as a special advisor dealing with sexism in advertising.
My hon. colleague talked about advertising and the media being a veiy important area where we have to root out sexism, so I am wondering what advice she is giving to her colleagues at Queen's Parks, on something which I was really shocked about. Perhaps, it goes to prove the point that violence against women exists not only in every sector of society, but within every political part of society as well. I wonder if my colleague could comment on that.

Mr. Speaker, the minister spoke about the Canada Assistance Plan, CAP, for the three wealthiest provinces, as she said. I would remind the minister that 46 per cent of the poor in Canada live in those three provinces.
The minister comes from the same province I do. She is familiar with the actions of the premier of British Columbia, Mr. Vander Zalm. She knows what is going on in British Columbia right now as that government disintegrates right before our veiy eyes. She knows what his position has been on the equality of women in society. If she is relying on the faith of Bill Vander Zalm to provide those shelters and to provide child care spaces, I would say she is sadly, sadly naive, because he is not going to do it and I think the minister knows that well.
She mentioned a situation that happened recently in Ontario where we saw the foolishness of a minister in the Ontario government posing as a "Sunshine Boy". It seemed very foolish to me. I agree with her.
The issue around his assistant or adviser, I think, is a much more serious issue. I think it was a very inappropriate appointment. I understand that Mr. Grimaldi has been removed from that position. I commend the Rae government for taking action quickly. I am not embarrassed to admit that New Democrats sometimes show poor judgement as well.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to compliment both the mover of the motion and particularly my colleague from New Westminster-Burnaby, the women's critic in our party. Certainly we have heard from all the speakers who have spoken so far of the need for the men in this Chamber and in the political system to grasp the issues that are at stake here and to get involved in these issues behind the 14 per cent of MPs who are women in this House.
Certainly the member needs to be credited by all women in our society and certainly by all of us who are interested in these issues for the role she has played not only within our caucus, but within the debate in Canada on these issues. I compliment her for making more of us aware of this issue in a much more constructive kind of way than many of us had been before.
There are two particular issues that I would like to raise with my colleague. First, she mentioned the economic factors that are involved. I would like to point out to her that in my constituency of Prince Albert-Churchill River, the federal government through the Department of Indian Affairs pays family assistance in a
March 13, 1991

community like Fond du Lac at about the level of $450 for a family of four.
Unfortunately, the economic circumstances are such that many people are on social assistance. The traditional economic base has eroded, as many people know. It is not the fault of those women and children living on that amount. The government recognized that in part and raised it another $100,1 believe, to about $550 because of the isolation.
However, there has been a study which indicates that it costs $950 in those communities just to feed a family of four in accordance with the Canada food rules, and all they get is $550. They are $400 a month short and that puts all kinds of pressure on those families. It causes family breakdowns, people moving to the cities and so on. It is strictly an economic matter that we are looking at.
In those communities they certainly welcomed the new initiative on family violence in Indian communities. However, we have a serious problem in that because of isolation and historic factors of one sort or another, it is very difficult to organize in those communities. You need to have proposals; you have to be able to deal with government bureaucracy. In a lot of these cases the kind of support to women that exists in many of the other communities and urban centres does not exist for these people.
We are talking here about people who not only face a gender problem, but also a race problem and a regional problem. I invite my colleague to address that question.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his question and his comments, particularly the one about the purpose I have served in our caucus, perhaps, of heightening the consciousness of some of my male colleagues in my own caucus. I appreciate that.
My colleague talks about a situation for rural women and native women in our society and outlined, I think very clearly, just what some women in Canada are up against, and how difficult it is in rural areas of Canada to provide these kinds of services and to get the community together in order to do that.
I think it is very important that when we are dealing with violence against native women in our society, as I said in my remarks, native women themselves must have
Supply
some control over the programs that are offered, over the way the transition home they want to start, or is started, operates.
I would point out too that economics, in my view, the fact that the gender gap in wages is widening, the fact that welfare rates in our country have not kept pace with inflation, has continued to serve to keep women down in these positions in our society.
In Vancouver there was a food bank established only for women and children. I think that is really a damning indication of what is happening to women and children in our society; a food bank simply, and only for, women and children.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Questions and comments are now terminated. Debate. The next two are 10 minutes, plus five minutes questions and comments.

Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House today compels me to speak to a subject that is painful, one that should not even be on this government's agenda in 1991 and should have ceased to exist years ago. I am referring to violence against women.
I know there are programs. I realize the federal government has just announced it will spend $136 million on measures to deal with family violence. However, I fail to understand how we could have let the situation become what it is today.
Mr. Speaker, violence against women has become almost common place. This is unacceptable. Unfortunately, respect for women is far from a foregone conclusion in any country.
Women represent half the world's population and work two thirds of all hours worked. They also constitute the largest group of poor, exploited individuals. One wonders how women an still be neglected to that extent in a world that claims to be increasingly civilized, a world that is exploring the outer edges of the universe.
Today, one would almost think technology seems more important than the basic well-being of human beings, especially human beings of the female sex.

March 13, 1991
Supply
Mr. Speaker, violence against women, which includes assault, mutilation, murder, infanticide, rape and criminal negligence, is probably the most widespread human rights issue but also the one that gets the least recognition. Why? Because it is so disturbing.
Each year in Canada, one woman out of eight at least-that is more than one million Canadian women- are abused by the man they live with. Women are victims of violence on the sole basis of their sex, and that remains a major obstacle to human growth. Unfortunately, too many women are considered as mere objects: luxury items, baby machines, domestics. If it sounds appalling, too bad! The fact remains that such is reality in this great country of ours. It is a fact of every day life for too many women.
Mr. Speaker, spousal abuse can take many forms. Women can be physically or sexually assaulted, emotionally and psychologically intimidated, degraded, deprived or exploited by their partners. Violence can leave not only visible marks on the body but also invisible emotional and psychological scars. The victim can feel terrorized, depressed, humiliated, desperate, shamed, abandoned and anxious.
Sadly, spousal abuse is an integral part of the Canadian society. It has become imperative that governments at all levels get involved to ensure the protection of Canadian women of all walks of life. They must get involved. No one must be allowed to abuse women in any way in Canada.
The federal government must relentlessly emphasize the greater welfare of the population. It must keep providing assistance to women groups, community organizations and front-line workers so that this problem can be eradicated by the end of the century.
Every woman must be allowed to play her role to the fullest in our society. Women must be allowed their dignity. The problem of spousal abuse must be dealt with urgently because, too often, it leads to family violence.

The campus reality is another area we must seriously look at. The use of sexist language in the classroom and educational materials, sexist articles in papers, demeaning graffiti, sexual harassment and assault are all part of
a vicious circle of attitudes and actions that send the wrong message about gender relations, at the expense of women. Why is it that some examples of sexism and violence against women on Canadian campuses make it into the news? Why do so many go unreported? What does this say of our society?
In most cases, after a headline everything is forgotten. In general, professors and the administration have done nothing to prevent or respond to sexism and violence against women. Things must change.
Slowly a few institutions are establishing sexual harassment policies and committees. It is a beginning, but it is only a beginning. It will not be able to go very far without financial assistance.
Federal and provincial governments have repeatedly cut back in funding for the operation of our universities and colleges. The federal budget announced this week continued this trend by extending the freeze on transfer payments to the provinces for health and education. In an already strained system campus initiatives to better the status of women will undoubtedly be among the first to be cut.

Mr. Speaker, battered and raped women need support and medical care. Funds are lacking. The government must respond to the urgent needs of such a large number of its citizens. Violence can only breed violence. Is this the future that we want to give our youth? Is this the vision of man that we want to give our daughters? No, Mr. Speaker. We must rethink our structures and, particularly, our priorities. We must consider these women who are at the roots of this country. They must be able to live without fear, without shame.
Poverty, misery, unemployment, illiteracy, these are all evils that can only increase the anger, the assaults, the rapes. It is unacceptable. We must put social problems at the top of this government agenda. We must give back to Canadian women their position in this society.
Mr. Speaker, it is a fact that the problem cannot be solved by legislation or by a government program, but the federal government must show leadership. It must mobilize and help fund those who are ready to make changes. It must show Canadian women that it takes the
March 13, 1991

problem seriously, but particularly, that it really wants to solve it.
A Royal Commission on Violence Against Women could be a welcome gesture and a sign of goodwill from this government. It has already been 20 years. It is time to re-examine the situation today.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, this evil must disappear so that every woman can regain her dignity and live with pride.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate my colleague from Saint-Laurent for a very thoughtful and sensitive speech on the motion before the House today, that this House call upon the Prime Minister to appoint a royal commission on violence against women.
I have a couple of questions which I think I can roll into one. A recent release of Amnesty International's report called Women on the Front Line outlines extreme violence against women's human rights. I wonder if the member could comment on whether this should be the mandate also of the royal commission, which would include discussion about the role Canada could play in the international community to combat violence against women.
Second, in speaking with a former colleague of mine from Saskatchewan, there is an increase in family violence in that province due to the horrible state of the farm economy. This is probably due to the high interest rates, the GATT issues, and all kinds of things like the weather. Many farms are going bankrupt and wife battering, child abuse and suicide are certainly on the increase in the farm community. The issue is that there is no place for women to go. Farm women and children are isolated even from their closest neighbour. There could be many miles between them. It is very difficult to keep track of the types of abuse that are going on in this situation. As I mentioned, most farmers cannot even see each other's houses and programs are not readily available for these women.
I am wondering if the royal commission could also look at ways to better provide services to the people of rural Canada. Will it be looking at putting in place a better
Supply
system of tracking violence against women in the situation I have just asked about?
I would like a response to these questions.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Nepean. When we are talking about a royal commission and about what Canada can do in the international community, I would be tempted to say that we have to start in our own community.
How can we possibly advise anyone in the international community? How can we possibly complain or criticize what is going on elsewhere when we have not been able to look at what is going on in our country?
Twenty years is a long time. Canada has changed a great deal in the last 20 years. I think we should be in a position to look at the international community as it touches violence against women, but first of all I would like us to look at our community.
I beg the ministers, since they are both here, to do something about this issue and to stop using bits and dregs of information that is out there. An in depth study has not been done with our cultural communities, and that is where a high level of violence is found.
I do not have any answers for families living in the western part of Canada, but I do know one thing. Coincidentally the member for Hamilton Mountain gave me her figures on increases in violence, in sex offences, and in assault. In 1987 the figures in just one Canadian city show 37 sexual assaults. In 1989, 536 in the same city and it is increasing. Normal assaults, which are not absolutely classified as sexual assaults, have probably increased in the same proportion.
This is why we need someone to work on this problem. Even though I realize the money has been given, we need to know where it could really be put to best use.

Mr. Speaker, I too am delighted to speak to the motion brought forward by my colleague from Halifax.
In part the motion reads:
That this House call upon the Prime Minister to appoint a royal
commission on violence against women.
Certainly the Liberal Party gives a tremendous amount of importance to this issue, and so we have taken this initiative and challenge to government.

March 13, 1991
Supply
It is hard for me, a man, to comprehend totally the feeling of fear the night holds for women. They are conditioned from birth to be wary. They learn to recognize situations that may hold harm.
Traditionally those situations have been connected to the night. An assailant attacks a woman alone in a secluded spot, a darkened area. Now tradition is changing. There are few situations today that do not hold harm and fear for a woman.
More and more often danger comes not in the shape of a stranger, but in the form of a woman's husband, son, male friend or date. Beatings and murders of women have increased phenomenally over the past five years. Terms like date rape, which I first heard in 1984, and gender violence, last year, are now being woven into our language.
The sanctuary of the home is becoming a myth. Sixty per cent of women murdered die at the hands of their partners. Twenty-five per cent of women had been sexually assaulted and abused, half before the age of 17, as reported by the National Action Committee on the Status of Women.
What of women who choose independent living? Do they feel safe living alone? At least 4 per cent of seniors are abused-and I am sure a good proportion of them are women too-by a family member at some time.
In 1989, 119 women were murdered by fists and knives, not by guns. And 75 per cent of the assailants were known. They happened at home, as reported by the December 1990 issue of the Canadian Forum.
I have heard of cases where young native women, hoping to escape abuse in the home, have turned to pregnancy and a subsequent welfare cheque as a means of escaping their homes and abuse. In fact, women on reservations and in remote aboriginal communities suffer a level of abuse that far exceeds the national level. They have nowhere to turn, nowhere to escape their abusers.
Fifty-two per cent of disabled women have been raped, assaulted or abused. This is truly a tragic commentary on our country. At least one in ten women is assaulted by her spouse or boyfriend.
The government has countered this flood of violence with its Family Violence Initiatives Program, a program that still falls short of delivering the solutions we need.
We must know the reasons behind the aggression of some men toward women. To understand the enemy, it has been said, is the best way to disarm the enemy.
Why does one man in ten assault his female partner? Who are these brutal men? They have to be accountable. What has led them to do the things they do? What are the best ways to help the victims of violence, most importantly? What more needs to be done?
Answers must be sought for these questions. The Minister of National Health and Welfare on February 20, 1991, in announcing the Family Violence Initiative, said in his opening statement: "I appeal for concerted national action on family violence".
In the previous December, I and many more of my Liberal colleagues called upon the government to create a royal commission on violence against women. We are asked: Why is there need for this commission? Let me attempt to answer that question.
First, I believe it will help Canadians to identify fully the spectrum of the causes of this grievous problem. On an individual basis we will know whether the poverty, insufficiency of income, unemployment, and poor education are related to insufficiency of government programs. We will also know whether they have the capacity to make a living, to buy a home and whether at times of crisis, illnesses, accidents, separation and divorce they have a transitional shelter to go to. We can examine whether as a society the government has been doing its job. Has the government been doing its job, for example, in the area of pornography trade and prostitution, just to mention one, that always is promoted on the backs of women who then become victims?
We will be able to ascertain the true magnitude of the problem. We will even be able to ascertain the age distribution in a very accurate way. Knowing the dimension of this problem will make us able to provide the proper approach-and it will give us a sense of the true gravity of this situation. It will tell us the nature of the problem, whether it is physical, sexual assault, psychological or even financial deprivation. It will tell us where violence occurs and what magnitude of that occurs in the homes, on the streets and even on school campuses. We will be able to examine the sequelae of this problem: The

y
March 13, 1991

immediate and the long-term. As the critic for health and welfare, I have discussed this issue with my associate critics, the member for Hamilton Mountain and the member for Mississauga. Truly, Mr. Speaker, when we imagine the sequelae of violence against women when they survive the physical violence, they end up having problems with alcohol and drug abuse, delinquency, prostitution, mental incapacitation and even suicide. When we fully appreciate the gravity of the problem, then perhaps this government will be compelled to truly take all the necessary steps.
We will be able to provide a comprehensive approach and not the piecemeal approach, and this is another value of a royal commission.
Last, Mr. Speaker, a royal commission during its process will be able to focus public awareness on this issue, sensitize Canadians, sensitize women as to the manifestations of violence, and even sensitize the media. The history of royal commissions on many other major issues in our country has taught us that great results have emanated from them.
We need great results to emanate from this proposed royal commission. It is worth an investment, Mr. Speaker. It is worth an investment. It will be a true signal lo Canadians that we are serious. It is wise and it is right and it is timely.

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - VIOLENCE AGAINST WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I came to the Department of National Health and Welfare I knew that family violence, and especially violence against women, was a serious problem in our culture, but I don't think I realized how deep and difficult a problem it would be to solve for each of us.
Many of our colleagues who have spoken in the debate before me have mentioned the ugly picture that is painted by statistics. They show that 10 per cent of women are assaulted by their male partners. We know that at least 25 per cent of girls are abused by the age of 16 and that about 60 per cent of the women murdered each year die at the hands of their partners.
These figures may well be conservative. Abused women are often too frightened to disclose the oppression they suffer. Experts estimate that the spoken or perceived threat of reprisal keeps more than half of the victims of abuse from speaking out and seeking help.
Violence against women is classic tyranny, and the tools of its perpetrators are entrapment, humiliation and intimidation. Victims of extreme cases become depersonalized, like survivors of other traumas. Efforts by victims to change the patterns of violence or to escape the offender are often met with increased threats of beatings and murder. The result is that women who have tried to escape and reorient their lives cannot be guaranteed safe haven in far too many cases.
Much of the violence against women takes place in the home. The family, the central unit of our society from which individuals gain their sense of security, compassion and self-esteem, is for many Canadian women a purgatory of rejection, manipulation and abuse. For far too many women, the family is experienced as a structure in which the supreme power of one over others is maintained through violence.
The abuse can be physical, sexual, psychological, emotional, or material. Some consequences of wife abuse, such as bruises and broken bones, are visible.
Shelter workers will attest to the pitiable condition in which some of their residents arrive, maimed and disfigured, when the violence they suffer finally drives them into hiding. Less evident, though often more severe, is the emotional and psychological damage the victims of wife abuse endure, wounds that never heal; terror and depression, hopelessness and isolation.
The reluctance of victims to speak about their abuse and the refusal of others to become involved creates a conspiracy of silence which protects the abuser. For far too long Canadians have been tempted to simply look away, to accept the brutal treatment of the innocent as someone else's problem, or to say that it is something that should be dealt with behind closed doors.
It is not someone else's problem. It belongs to all of us. If we simply look the other way, we are complicit in acts of violence which leave the victims intimidated, sexually assaulted, molested, beaten, tortured and, far too frequently, dead.
The question that begs a response is: What twisted logic makes some men think that they can abuse women? The answer is elusive, but clearly social values and conventions which do not assure equal rights and status to women, children and seniors make them vulnerable to violence in the family. Traditional views which deem men to be the head of their household, demand that women honour and obey their husbands, and insist that children be seen and not heard are major factors in the cultural permission that men feel when they channel their emotions through a tunnel of violence.
In the past, action to protect the victims of abuse, apprehend and punish the offenders, and address the root causes of family violence has been slow to evolve.
Women's groups have long stressed the importance of protection and shelter for battered women and their children. They have taken a leading role both in developing a response to the needs of the victims and in promoting general understanding of the nature of violence itself.
Their efforts have been fruitful and tireless, since the first shelter was opened in British Columbia in 1972. We now have over 300 shelters in Canada.
March 13, 1991

Point of Order
The late 1970s in Canada saw widespread legislative reform of family law, particularly matrimonial property law, aided by a new cohort of feminist lawyers working toward recognition of marriage as a partnership of equals.
Among the federal responses to the problem of family violence in the 1980s was the Badgely report in 1984 which examined the adequacy of laws designed to protect the vulnerable. On the basis of that report and for the first time in this country's history the government of Canada addressed family violence as a matter of national concern in the Speech from the Throne.

In 1986, the federal government launched a $25 million five-year Child Sexual Abuse program and, two years later, a $40 million four-year Family Violence Initiative.
We built new shelters. We learned how to train people to deal with family violence. We conducted research and learned a great deal about the extent and nature of violence against women.
We funded more than 700 projects, each of which had a practical and measurable objective. Under Project Haven, for instance, which is administered by the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, up to 500 new shelter units are being created for abused women and their children.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - VIOLENCE AGAINST WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is very gracious of you to recognize me again.

Mr. Speaker, the federal Women's Film Program was supported in its effort to produce and distribute films related to women's issues. The Disabled Women's Network was funded to conduct workshops with transition house staff, raising awareness about the vulnerability of women to abuse.
The Canadian Teacher's Federation was able to distribute to its member network the resource "Thumbs Down-A Classroom Response to Violence Against Women." And 56,000 Canadian physicians received a special adaptation of the Ontario Medical Association's "Reports on Wife Assault."
Today in every jurisdiction in Canada we have mechanisms to address family violence and our common efforts
have led us to loudly reaffirm a central value of our society-that violence, in any form, is unacceptable. We recognize that violence in Canada is a serious, pervasive and intolerable ill. Will recognize also that it is a national problem, one that will require nothing less than a national response if we are to succeed in a significant way. This is society's problem. No law or program enacted by government can make it disappear. What government can do, however, is to provide leadership and to help to mobilize the efforts of countless individuals, agencies and organizations to make a concerted and sustained effort to stop the suffering. Last month we did just that when we announced a new Family Violence Initiative, one designed to build on the experience of the past four years and to encourage new approaches and alliances.

Mr. Speaker, I listened earlier as my colleague from New Westminster-Burnaby mentioned in her remarks the fact that this new initiative on family violence would amount to $136 million in new funds, a figure that she dismissed as a mere drop in the bucket.
For the women who are suffering from family violence and for the others who are all too often its victims, this $136 million in new funds is important and welcomed news, indeed.
When members opposite denigrate the role of the federal government in dealing with issues related to family violence, they should be aware of the fact that through our contributions in health care, through our contributions through the Canada Assistance Plan, through direct spending we are making under the family violence program, we are spending, likely, in excess of a billion dollars a year to provide assistance to victims of family violence. That is an important contribution that is made by this Parliament and by the federal government.
I listened, but listened without success, to hear colleagues on the other side make suggestions for ways that we could be more effective in terms of targeting that money. I listened for concrete suggestions and new initiatives that could be taken and new ways in which we could assist the victims of family violence, or that we could intervene today to prevent the cycle of family violence from continuing for yet another generation.
March 13, 1991

What we have heard from the other side is two things: first, that we should simply be increasing the amount of money, that $136 million is trivial; and second, that instead of acting what we should be doing is studying.
I listened to my colleague and friend from Winnipeg as he gave his remarks a few minutes ago in calling for more study, as his colleagues did as well. Elow much more study is needed for us to recognize that all too often women and children are left in situations that are abusive because they have no place to go?
How much more study is needed before we recognize that family violence is part of a cycle that carries on from generation to generation and that it is essential for us to act now to break that cycle?
How much more study is needed before we recognize that there are problems all too often in our courts in an insensitivity to the needs of victims of family violence, or should we be acting now?
How much more study is needed before we come to the conclusion that policies in the past, that have required that women who have been abused in homes would have to lay the charges, were wrong and that police officers should be given instructions when they are called to domestic disputes that they should lay the charges? We do not need more study of that, we need action.
How much more study is needed before we are able to conclude that measures have to be taken to look at the portrayal of women and children in the media, to recognize the fact that all too often that portrayal diminishes their humanity, reduces their worth and allows them to be abused? Need we study that further, or can we act today to deal with this sort of a problem?
That is what the policy on family violence is designed to do. It is designed to build on the enormous reservoir of talent that there is in this country, on the commitment, which is growing at all levels in our society across Canada at all levels of government and throughout society, that recognizes that it is time today, not two years hence, but today for attitudes to change, for programs to be put in place, for all of us to recognize that this is society's problem and that all of us are involved. Let us not wait until later to do it, let us act now.
Supply
That is why that $136 million in new funds is so very important. That is why the other legislative initiatives that were disclosed in the Family Violence Program will be so important for Canadians as well because we can act today. We do have the data that we need to make significant progress and we will learn more. We will learn more from studies, there is no question about that, but there is no excuse for us not taking action today, action which will help to stem the suffering and the loss of life of far too many people.
The evidence is there. It is incontrovertible. It is powerful. The silent suffering of so many women across Canada implores us to take action at this level in this Parliament to provide leadership today and not years from now.

Mr. Speaker, if the strategy is to be successful it must serve as a catalyst for action, part of a series of initiatives at different levels of government and society which are needed to combat deeply rooted societal attitudes.
Consequently we undertook a massive series of consultations with provincial and territorial governments and the non-government sector. We consulted widely with all levels of government, women's groups, child advocacy organizations, senior's groups, front-line service providers, professional associations and researchers.
In June of 1989, we hosted a National Forum on Family Violence to identify major issues and suggest avenues for activity.
The result is a new program which will make available $136 million, in new funds, over the next four years, more than twice the level of funding currently committed by the federal government to address the problem of violence.
The federal strategy has three main objectives: to combat the attitudes and stereotypes that encourage and excuse this senseless violence, to ensure that the brutal people who commit these acts are called to account, and, most importantly, to provide help to the innocent victims who, all too often, are asked to bear their cruel burden in silence.
Through the initiative the Government will strengthen intervention and treatment services by training RCMP recruits, and the staffs of Correctional Services Canada

March 13, 1991
Supply
and the National Parole Board to better understand the patterns of violence faced by women.
Training materials will be developed and supported for judges, physicians, nurses and social workers-both those who appear in court and those who work on the front lines. Of major urgency, availability of housing for victims will be substantially improved. Treatment will be provided to violent and sexual offenders in all 60 federal correctional institutions.

Today in Vancouver my colleague, the Minister of Justice, is announcing the government's plans to review provisions of the Criminal Code, the Divorce Act and other legislation with regard to pornography, the adequacy of current bail provisions and the forcible removal of offenders from the home. This is action which should be taken now to begin this and not waiting until later.
Within my own department we will fund community projects designed to treat and prevent abuse, train physicians and social workers, collect and disseminate information and conduct research and evaluation. The national clearing house on family violence will receive an almost fourfold budgetary increase, enabling it to build upon existing resources and improve public access to its materials.
We will continue our support to the National Film Board family violence collection, a collection of videos which have been seen by 8.5 million Canadians. We are not waiting until later, this is action that needs to be taken now.
In consultation with aboriginal communities, we will train 2,000 health care and social service workers serving Indian reserves and Inuit communities, relying upon their help to develop prevention programs in over 500 communities.
Undoubtedly, the most important element of this initiative is to serve as a catalyst for all of society to mobilize its resources to pull together to deal with this issue. It is not a federal government issue; it is a national problem in which all of us-governments, the private sector, voluntary agencies and individuals-must share together. All must work together. All of us must mobilize what resources we can find to deal with the problem that is pervasive, that cuts across all demographic and geographic lines in our society and a problem which
causes suffering and, in too many instances, death on the part of its innocent victims.
That is the plea that I make today to members of the Flouse: not to put things off until later, not to say that we do not have enough information to know that this problem is pervasive or to know that there are measures we can take today to begin to bring down the level of this violence, but for us all to work with all sectors of society starting today, to mobilize those resources, to change attitudes, to begin to ensure that the human worth and dignity of every Canadian is respected and to begin to bring down that level of violence in our society and to ensure that those people who suffer the senseless violence receive the aid and assistance that they so desperately need.
By working together, we can do precisely that. No issue is more fundamental for this Parliament, no issue more demands action today than that we work together on this. Studies, yes; studies will continue. But it is essential that we commit ourselves today to acting today before more innocent victims have to suffer for our failures.

I do not believe we are building on sand. I believe that we are building on a bedrock of co-operation which will have profound effects in improving the quality of life for Canadians.

speakeroldname: Ms. Nicole Roy-Arcelin (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - VIOLENCE AGAINST WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the beginning of this debate, the opposition has been saying the government is indifferent or seems to be indifferent to the problems facing women. Mr. Speaker, it so happens we are very much aware of what the government is doing to deal with the disastrous effects of violence against women.
Perhaps the minister could expand somewhat on the program he announced a few weeks ago, a program that in my opinion is taking great strides towards eliminating violence against women.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - VIOLENCE AGAINST WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, indeed I would be glad to do that.
What we have done is take an initiative which involves some six different departments of government. It is a designed deal at the criminal level with people who are abusers. It is designed to ensure that there are services made available to offenders to try to train them and to try to rehabilitate them. It is designed to provide assis-
