tance to people who suffer from family violence. It is designed to build partnerships with groups in the private sector, non-governmental organizations, to work together to try to change attitudes and to provide services. It is designed to activate networks at the provincial and local levels, which can be important in terms of making people more aware of when family violence occurs and how to deal with it. It is designed to build upon services through police officers, Correctional Service Canada and the National Parole Board to ensure that offenders guilty of family violence either receive the treatment that is necessary or that measures are taken to ensure that their victims are properly protected from them.
It is designed to look at issues which all too often take a woman and children who have been abused out of the home and leave the abuser still in the home, with them losing both their whole way of life and their home.
Through this concerted action we are confident that we can have an important impact on the level of violence from which far too many women in this society suffer.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - VIOLENCE AGAINST WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to start by congratulating the member for Halifax on proposing this motion today.
We have gone through a period of time over recent weeks and months, in which the attention of virtually all Canadians was glued to one issue and almost nothing else. Of course I am referring to the war in the Persian Gulf. In that period of time other issues that we could have and perhaps even should have been talking about were not raised as much as they could have been.
That does not mean to say that everyone in public office or even advocacy groups did not do their jobs. Even in instances when very important issues were raised, the attention of the media and Canadians generally was focused in another direction. To a degree, raising important issues that should have received much attention was sometimes like whistling in the wind.
Our colleague from Halifax reminds us today of an important topic that indeed should have been raised in the House before and has been raised in the House before by her and others. She has been very vigilant in raising issues involving family violence, and more particularly violence against women. A few weeks ago she raised criticism involving the minister's initiative. She

March 13, 1991
Supply
has questioned the government on several occasions, and I congratulate her for that.

Mr. Speaker, the subject before the House today is a sad one. I think it is appropriate that both men and women are speaking to this issue in the House today. We are talking about violence against women, but we are also talking about the violence perpetrated by men against women. Of course, in most cases when we talk about violence in this connection, we are talking about violence by men against women, and that is what we are talking about today.
I am not proud of the fact, Mr. Speaker, and think it should be repeated over and over again, in this House and elsewhere, until such time that men, both collectively and individually, realize that violence against women is unacceptable and that it must stop.

As late as the end of the last century, women, once married, were considered to be chattels of their husbands, a form of property. Perhaps some of that mindset is regrettably still there among some people today, treating indeed their wife or partner or significant other, however one wants to put it, as being their property.
The issue in question has been studied a lot. The minister has referred to that. However, if it has been studied so successfully and if all has been done, why is the problem still there? Why is the problem still there in the numbers and magnitude that we know that it is? Obviously we do not have all the answers. I would like to think that if the minister had all the answers he could have given us all the solutions. If any of us had all the answers we could have provided all the solutions and the problem would be gone. But it is not; the problem is still there in very large numbers.
In my previous incarnation in politics, if I may put it that way, when I was a member of the Ontario legislature, I was the social policy spokesperson for our party. We had a study by the Ontario legislature committee on social development, on violence against women. Day after day we listened to testimony from women's groups, even on occasion from battering husbands. There were days in which the evidence was virtually impossible to listen to. There were days on which I had to walk out of
the committee room several times during the deliberations because it was just so awful to hear.
It is almost a decade ago. As a matter of fact, as I look now at the calendar in front of us on the clerks' table, I notice that we are only six days away from my 10th anniversary of my election to Queen's Park, March 19, 1981. It was shortly after that that we had this study. Ten years have gone by, or close to it, and yet the problem is still there.
I do not accept the minister's argument that the request of my colleague from Halifax is unreasonable. I do not accept his comment that we have all the answers now and that there is no need to have this royal commission.
I am paraphrasing his words earlier. He said: "We don't need to study the issue further. We can act today". If that is true, I will have to back up one day and pretend we are on March 12, 1991 and say that if we could act today, why did we not act yesterday or the day before? Presumably if as of half an hour ago the minister had all those answers that he was referring to, he must have had them for sometime. He must have had them yesterday or a week ago or at some other period of time.
I am not blaming the minister in the sense that I hold him responsible for the violence that exists. That would be unfair and untrue, but I do blame the minister for that attitude of saying that we do not need to revisit this issue again and to study it further.
I am the first one to criticize expenditures on government use or sometimes overuse of royal commissions on a variety of issues. I can say as an opposition critic on government expenditures that I certainly would not criticize the principle of having such an expenditure now. The issue is of such import that all members of the House should join together and request that royal commission by the government.
It is my hope that the government, notwithstanding the remarks only moments ago of the minister, will undertake such a study on family violence and violence against women particularly.
As I indicated to you a little earlier, Mr. Speaker, I wish to share my time with our colleague, the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond. With that I will end my comments and I will look forward to the contribution by my colleague from Cape Breton-East

Richmond who is the former critic of this very important issue for our caucus.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique B. Tardif (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Supply and Services):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - VIOLENCE AGAINST WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I should like to remind my colleague that in the previous Parliament the government did take the first step concerning family violence.
I do not know whether he remembers that. The first step has been made. The government has decided to give priority to this matter and continue to take action.
Mr. Speaker, I must admit that I fully agree with the minister's position. Perhaps I should draw my colleague's attention to last Sunday's Martine Corriveau editorial in Le Soldi entitled "No more commissions of inquiry".
She was referring to the request made by the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women to have such a commission appointed. She said about this request that "the least one can say is that it lacks originality and raises suspicions".
I will not read the whole editorial, but she went on to say: "If we are to review past experiences, analyze current data, consult university research projects and explore new ways of intervening, there are procedures lest costly and probably more effective than referring the issue to an inquiry commission, royal though it might be".
We need evidence and opinions? Why not use the very simple tools available to the first human democracies, such as informal meetings, genuine citizens' forums, sectorial sessions chaired by advocacy people from various fields of activities in each county, each region, and each province?
She concluded that "the millions of dollars saved could be used to reduce the deficit, eliminating one cause of economic violence against Canadian society as a whole".
Mr. Speaker, what I want to know from my colleague is how, at a time when we seek to give priority to measures designed to reduce violence, would we proceed with a study which would only delay any action we might take to repress violence?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81 - VIOLENCE AGAINST WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the short time that I have I do want to be on the record in support of my colleague from Halifax who has called upon the government to commission a royal commission with regard to the violence against women.
It was approximately 15 months ago that a troubled young man, full of blind hatred and unfounded fears and armed with a semi-automatic rifle, marched into the Ecole Polytechnique at the University of Montreal. The cold, insane reality of that day saw him go after young women in the hallways and classrooms of the engineering school last December 6 and trumpeting his rage brutally cut down 14 young, innocent female students.
Surely those young women, in the fleeting moments of their lives, must have felt a fear that men my age and perhaps your age, Mr. Speaker, cannot fully appreciate or understand.
It is the fear that a woman feels when she is walking from her in a dark and lonely underground parking garage and hears the hollow sound of footsteps close behind. It is the fear a woman feels when late at night her husband or boyfriend comes home drunk, angry, full of violence and unrepentant rage. It is the fear a woman feels when she is walking alone on a quiet sidewalk in the chilly early evening and sees her own shadow cast by the street lights being overtaken by someone else's presence. It is a fear that seizes you in the stomach and it is a fear marked by terror and by tears.
But violence against women is much more, much more than a lone gunman stalking the hallways of a school or a rapist lurking in the shadows of a quiet street. Violence against women occurs everywhere: at the work place, in the home and on the street. It can occur unfortunately at any time.

March 13, 1991
Supply
The attacker can be wearing jeans and a tee-shirt or outfitted in a dark grey flannel suit. Sometimes the abuse is between a husband and a wife and sometimes it is the corporate executive who earns $80,000 a year.
I will give an example. There is the man who picked up his wife of 32 years at the restaurant where she had worked and said he had to take her to a lawyer's office to sign the divorce papers. Instead, he took her to an isolated field, killed her and then he killed himself.
There is the young woman, the young mother and her little boy. I defended individuals such as these. They were both very much alone, getting ready to move out after five months of living in a shelter for battered women. You can picture it, Mr. Speaker. The room is filled almost to the ceiling with green plastic garbage bags that contain their clothes and other belongings. But they have courage, confidence in a new start and growing hope for a better life.
Finally, in those two moments that I have, sometimes the abuse is rape.
It is the 16-year old girl, just an average person, a so-so athlete and a mediocre student but friendly and outgoing. She loves being with her friends, listening to a few tunes and partying on the weekend. But one Friday night she is out at a party and the parents are not at home. What starts out as a handful of young people hanging out in the family room, gathered around the
stereo, turns into a crowd of over 100 teenagers and young adults. There is beer, hard liquor and cheap wine.
The 16-year old girl has agreed to have a drink, and the drinks keep coming. In the early morning hours she is dragged upstairs to a bedroom by three or four of the older boys, boys she does not go to school with, boys she does not even know. She does not know what is happening to her. She is raped and she passes out. She is left all alone in a strange room until sometime later in the day when she can find her own way home.
It happens, Mr. Speaker. It happens all too often.
When I see the list of organizations in this country that have called for a royal commission on violence against women, from the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women-and I want to table this list with my remarks-I cannot see any justification in any government, regardless of one's partisan political affiliation, for not having a royal commission which can thoroughly discuss the issues and, more important, Mr. Speaker, as I am sure you would agree as a father and a husband, and I as a father of two girls, would want to know the real causes of family violence against women.
